subject: model
value: The full extracted plain text of one catalogued PDF, stored as a 1:1 extension of its documents row.
justification: The DDL makes this a pure 1:1 extension table: doc_id is simultaneously PRIMARY KEY and the FK to documents(id) with ON DELETE CASCADE, so one row is the text of exactly one document and text is payload, never an identifier. The open uniqueness subject 'text' is rejected: documents carries text_ok/text_error/text_chars precisely because extraction can fail, and any two failed or near-empty extractions collide; two byte-identical PDFs stored at different paths (the case duplicate_sets exists to record) would also carry identical text. Uniqueness over six long extractions is incidental. Scope is current-state, not per-build or historical: manifest.json states 'catalog.sqlite is canonical' while manifest.json itself is the generated summary, so the DB is the maintained authority rather than a build log; the row mirrors whatever PDF sits at documents.path right now, and re-extraction after that file is replaced rewrites the same row (documents.path is UNIQUE, so no path can accumulate a history of texts). No mvd subjects were raised and observed_mvds is empty.

subject: *all-unruled*
justification: 43 rows, 36 columns, 567 FDs. 13 columns are constant ([] -> source_group, source_subgroup, topic, suggested_folder, title_source, author_source, needs_title_review, inference_notes, year_source, pdfinfo_ok/error, text_ok/error); 14 more are 43-distinct row serials (id, path, filename, size_bytes, sha256, title, text_chars, text_path, suggested_name, inferred_title, original_filename, original_path, standard_filename, what_it_does) because the corpus is one hand-curated PDF per row, renamed 'YYYY - Author - Title.pdf'. Only 9 columns carry information. Of the 28 genuinely unruled determinants, 25 have zero repeat groups -- no test at all. The 3 with any repetition are tested by at most 4 rows, and what those rows agree on is blank: producer,original_title,inferred_author fixes pages on 3 rows whose original_title is ''; producer,original_author,publication_year fixes original_title='' twice. venue -> publication_year reads a year out of free text (41/43 venues contain it literally) across two groups of two. Count note: the packet's 41 overstates -- 12 of the 40 sampled were already ruled accidental under a different column ordering (author,original_author,pages vs pages,author,original_author), so 28 remain. I concur with those 12 prior rulings.

subject: author
justification: NOT a sparsity artifact -- a structural duplication artifact, and the distinction matters for the remedy. Measured: author = inferred_author in 43 of 43 rows (byte-identical), with author_source = 'surflab-html+agent' uniformly. The inference step wrote the same value into both columns, so this FD is a tautology of copying and would still hold at 43,000 rows. But `author` names no entity: it is a free-text concatenated byline ('Jorg Peters, Meera Sitharam, Yong Zhou, JianHua Fan'), not a person or an author record. Promoting it would mint a bogus authors lookup keyed on a multi-author string. Correct remedy is dropping one redundant column, not extracting a table.

subject: author,original_author,pages
justification: Composite of a free-text byline, a mostly-empty legacy PDF-metadata field (original_author is '' in 28 of 43 rows), and a page count. 43 rows against columns with 16-24 distinct values each makes any triple near-unique. Page counts and blank metadata identify nothing; this measures the table's sparsity.

subject: author,original_author,producer
justification: producer is the PDF toolchain build string ('pdfTeX-1.40.20', 'Aladdin Ghostscript 5.50') -- 28 distinct values over 43 rows, pure generator bookkeeping. Combined with a byline and a field that is empty in 28 of 43 rows, the triple is essentially unique by construction. Nothing here owns a title or a page count.

subject: author,original_author,publication_year
justification: publication_year has 24 distinct values over 43 rows (max group 4); original_author is '' in 28 of 43. The triple is near-unique, so it 'determines' original_title, pages and producer only because almost no two rows share it. A year is a categorical bucket, not an identifier.

subject: author,original_title,producer
justification: original_title is legacy PDF-metadata junk -- '' in 19 rows and the dvips default 'p.dvi' in 6 more, i.e. 25 of 43 rows carry no real title. Paired with a byline and a toolchain build string, the triple collides almost never. Determining `pages` from it is sparsity, not ownership.

subject: author,original_title,publication_year
justification: Same shape: junk original_title (25 of 43 rows are '' or 'p.dvi') plus a byline plus a year with 24 distinct values. Near-unique composite; page count and producer are per-file facts owned by the file, reachable via path/id, not by this triple.

subject: author,pages,producer
justification: Textbook accidental composite: a byline plus two pieces of unrelated bookkeeping (page count, generator build string). Counts and toolchain versions do not identify anything -- they collide rarely across 43 rows and that is all this dependency measures.

subject: creation_date
justification: Near-unique timestamp column -- 38 distinct values over 43 rows, the only repeat being '' (6 rows). A PDF creation timestamp determines everything downstream simply because it almost never repeats. It is also the wrong direction: a timestamp is an attribute of the file, not an owner of its author metadata.

subject: creation_date,producer
justification: Superset of an already near-unique timestamp column (38/43 distinct), widened by the generator build string. Guaranteed near-unique; the FD to original_title carries no information about the domain.

subject: creation_date,publication_year
justification: Same near-unique timestamp (38/43 distinct) padded with a year. The composite is unique in effect, and original_title is in any case junk metadata ('' or 'p.dvi' in 25 of 43 rows).

subject: filename -> author,creation_date,id,inferred_author,inferred_title,original_author,original_filename,original_path,original_title,pages,path,producer,publication_year,sha256,size_bytes,standard_filename,suggested_name,text_chars,text_path,title,venue,what_it_does
justification: Representative of the naming block -- filename, text_path, suggested_name, original_filename, original_path, standard_filename, all 43 distinct with zero repeat groups. MANIFEST.md records that every PDF was renamed to 'YYYY - Author - Title.pdf', so these basenames are unique because a curator made them unique in a 43-file directory, not because a basename owns a document. Only path, the declared key, is unique by construction. Zero testing groups is zero evidence.

subject: id -> author,creation_date,filename,inferred_author,inferred_title,original_author,original_filename,original_path,original_title,pages,path,producer,publication_year,sha256,size_bytes,standard_filename,suggested_name,text_chars,text_path,title,venue,what_it_does
justification: The declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and an already-adjudicated intended key. A surrogate row identifier owns every attribute of the document row by definition, in every legal state of the catalogue, not merely in this instance. Its closure is not evidence of sparsity; it is the meaning of a primary key.

subject: inferred_author
justification: The mirror image of the `author` candidate and accidental for the same structural reason, not a small-sample one: inferred_author = author in 43 of 43 rows, so each trivially determines the other. This records exact column duplication left by the title/author-inference migration (inferred_*, original_*, *_source were added later), not an entity. A concatenated byline owns nothing; drop the redundant column rather than extracting a relation.

subject: inferred_author,original_author,pages
justification: Byte-identical twin of the 'author,original_author,pages' candidate, since inferred_author equals author in every row. That the packet lists both is direct evidence it is enumerating column combinations rather than reporting independent facts. Accidental sparsity on top of a duplicated column.

subject: inferred_author,original_author,producer
justification: Twin of 'author,original_author,producer' (inferred_author = author in 43/43). Composite of a duplicated byline, a field empty in 28 of 43 rows, and a PDF generator build string -- near-unique over 43 rows, identifying nothing.

subject: inferred_author,original_author,publication_year
justification: Twin of 'author,original_author,publication_year'. Near-unique triple over a 43-row table; a publication year is a bucket and original_author is blank in 28 of 43 rows. Sparsity, not schema.

subject: inferred_author,original_title,publication_year
justification: Twin of 'author,original_title,publication_year'. original_title is toolchain junk ('' 19 rows, dvips default 'p.dvi' 6 rows); combined with a duplicated byline and a year the triple almost never repeats.

subject: inferred_author,pages,producer
justification: Twin of 'author,pages,producer'. A duplicated byline plus two unrelated bookkeeping columns -- page count and generator version. Counts and toolchain strings do not identify a document; path and id do.

subject: original_author,pages,publication_year
justification: The widest sparsity artifact in this relation: it 'owns' four attributes only because original_author is '' in 28 of 43 rows while pages (24 distinct) and publication_year (24 distinct) split the remainder almost uniquely. Nothing about a blank legacy metadata field plus a page count plus a year names an entity.

subject: original_title
justification: Cleanest disproof in the packet. original_title has exactly two multi-row groups: '' (19 rows) and 'p.dvi' (6 rows) -- 'p.dvi' being the default title dvips stamps into PDFs it generates. Both groups have original_author = '' throughout, so the entire FD is witnessed by 25 rows of blank-and-junk metadata agreeing on another blank. Every genuine original_title value is unique, so the dependency is never actually tested. This is PDF-toolchain junk, not a title owning an author.

subject: original_title,pages,producer
justification: Built on the same junk column (25 of 43 rows are '' or the dvips default 'p.dvi') plus a page count and a generator build string. Near-unique triple; determining author and inferred_author from it is doubly hollow since those two columns are identical copies.

subject: original_title,pages,publication_year
justification: Same junk original_title, widened with two bookkeeping columns of 24 distinct values each. The triple is effectively unique over 43 rows, and two of the three 'owned' attributes (author, inferred_author) are the same column twice.

subject: pages,producer,publication_year
justification: The archetype the brief warns about: a composite of three unrelated bookkeeping columns -- a page count, a PDF generator build string, and a year -- claiming to own four attributes. None of the three identifies anything; over 43 rows they simply never collide. Approving this would turn PDF-toolchain noise into schema.

subject: pages,venue -> author,creation_date,filename,id,inferred_author,inferred_title,original_author,original_filename,original_path,original_title,path,producer,sha256,size_bytes,standard_filename,suggested_name,text_chars,text_path,title,what_it_does
justification: Representative of the ten sampled composites built on a near-unique column: every pairing of venue (41 distinct) or creation_date (38 distinct) with anything reaches 43 distinct in 43 rows and zero repeat groups. Adding a page count to an almost-unique free-text venue produces a key by exhaustion. A composite that never collides has never been tested.

subject: path -> author,creation_date,filename,id,inferred_author,inferred_title,original_author,original_filename,original_path,original_title,pages,producer,publication_year,sha256,size_bytes,standard_filename,suggested_name,text_chars,text_path,title,venue,what_it_does
justification: Declared TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE and the other already-adjudicated intended key. An absolute filesystem path names exactly one catalogued file, so it owns that file's scan record. This is the natural key the whole catalogue is built on, and it stays unique by construction as the corpus grows -- unlike every other 43-distinct column here.

subject: producer,original_author,publication_year -> original_title
justification: Two groups of two rows, and in both the agreed value of original_title is the empty string -- original_author is '' in 28 of 43 rows and original_title is '' in 19 more, so this records two pairs of rows agreeing that legacy PDF metadata is absent. Confirming a blank is not confirming a dependency. The determinant combines a generator build string, a mostly-empty field, and a four-digit year bucket (24 distinct over 43 rows); it holds by collision scarcity.

subject: producer,original_title,inferred_author -> pages
justification: One of only three unruled determinants with any repeat group, and the group disproves it. Its single group is 3 rows sharing producer 'pdfTeX-1.40.20', inferred_author 'Kestutis Karciauskas, Jorg Peters', and original_title '' -- that is, three papers by the same pair, built by the same TeX release, whose legacy PDF title metadata is blank. They agree on pages=11 by coincidence of length. A PDF toolchain build string plus a blank metadata field plus a byline identifies no entity and cannot own a page count.

subject: sha256 -> author,creation_date,filename,id,inferred_author,inferred_title,original_author,original_filename,original_path,original_title,pages,path,producer,publication_year,size_bytes,standard_filename,suggested_name,text_chars,text_path,title,venue,what_it_does
justification: The most tempting near-key, and the schema refutes it in its own words: this database carries duplicate_sets(sha256, count, paths_json), a table whose existence declares that one content hash may cover several paths. It is empty today, which is exactly why sha256 has 43 distinct values in 43 rows and zero repeat groups -- the claim is never tested once. A content hash cannot own path, id, filename, original_path, suggested_name or standard_filename, which are the location and naming facts duplicate_sets exists to hold apart from it.

subject: title -> author,creation_date,filename,id,inferred_author,inferred_title,original_author,original_filename,original_path,original_title,pages,path,producer,publication_year,sha256,size_bytes,standard_filename,suggested_name,text_chars,text_path,venue,what_it_does
justification: Free text, 43 distinct in 43 rows, zero repeat groups. Its apparent ownership of inferred_title is a copying tautology, not ownership: title is byte-identical to inferred_title on all 43 rows because title_source is uniformly 'surflab-html+agent'. The sibling corpus on this identical schema (DAFX, 1457 rows, title_source in {pdfinfo, filename}) shows the two columns diverge as a matter of course -- author differs from inferred_author on 1119 of its rows. A free-text title is a near-key, not an owner.

subject: venue -> publication_year
justification: The only unruled single-column determinant with any repetition, and it is worth nothing: 41 distinct venues in 43 rows, two groups of two. Both groups agree on the year because the venue string literally contains it -- 'Mathematical Methods for Curves and Surfaces (MMCS, Oslo) 2012 / Springer LNCS' and 'Preprint (Elsevier), 2023' -- as do 41 of 43 rows. So this inverts a substring rather than naming an entity that owns an attribute, and it is refuted in the instance already: the two venues that omit the year ('Int. J. Computational Geometry & Applications (IJCGA)' -> 2011, 'talk slides (companion to Axioms 2014 paper)' -> 2013) show a venue that recurs across years cannot carry one. Free text with an embedded year is a near-key.

subject: what_it_does -> author,creation_date,filename,id,inferred_author,inferred_title,original_author,original_filename,original_path,original_title,pages,path,producer,publication_year,sha256,size_bytes,standard_filename,suggested_name,text_chars,text_path,title,venue
justification: An agent-written prose sentence describing each paper ('Curved PN Triangles: closed-form cubic triangular Bezier patch...'), 43 distinct in 43 rows, zero repeat groups. Free-text commentary authored one-per-row is the purest form of near-key: it is unique precisely because someone wrote a different sentence for each row. It names nothing and owns nothing.

subject: model
value: One PDF currently held in the render/non-euclidean corpus, with its file facts, PDF metadata, agent-curated title/author/venue inference, and intake provenance.
justification: The DDL declares both keys: id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and path TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, path being the corpus-relative natural key. sha256 is deliberately not a key — documents_sha256_idx is a plain index and the sibling duplicate_sets(sha256 PRIMARY KEY, count, paths_json) exists precisely to record one hash spanning several paths — so observed uniqueness of sha256, size_bytes, pages, text_chars and creation_date is only an artifact of six distinct files. filename, standard_filename, suggested_name and suggested_folder are derived renaming fields that merely approximate path; identical filenames in different folders are legal, and suggested_folder is already constant. title, inferred_title, venue, what_it_does and producer are descriptive metadata. Every flagged combination built on original_title or original_author is already fragile: both are '' on ids 3, 4 and 6 and producer is '' on id 5, so those pairs collapse the moment another metadata-less PDF arrives. original_path/original_filename record intake provenance and are nullable. Scope is current-state: manifest.json names catalog.sqlite canonical (not a build log), size/sha256/pages describe the file at path now, and UNIQUE(path) forbids the append-only history a provenance record would require.

subject: model
value: One content hash that occurs at more than one path in the corpus, with how many paths hold it and the list of those paths.
justification: The table is empty, so discovery supplies nothing; the DDL settles it. sha256 TEXT PRIMARY KEY makes the content hash the identifier, with count and paths_json as payload: one row is one hash plus the corpus paths holding those bytes. It is the counterpart of documents.sha256, which is intentionally non-unique (documents_sha256_idx is a plain index) — this is where a hash appearing at several paths gets recorded, which is also why sha256 cannot be a key of documents. No column was offered as an atomicity candidate because there are no rows, but paths_json is by construction a repeating group: several path facts about one hash, properly a duplicate_paths(sha256, path) child, from which count is derivable. Scope is current-state: it is a derived duplicate report over the inventory documents describes now, and it is empty only because all six current files hash distinctly; adding a copy of an existing PDF would populate it. No mvd subjects. needs_user is false — zero rows plus a self-describing DDL is still decisive.

subject: doc_id,locator
justification: Measured: across 180 rows, exactly ONE (doc_id, locator) group has more than one row -- (doc_id=11, 'Section 2, Lemma 1', 2 rows). The FD is witnessed by a single pair of rows out of 180; 179 rows never test it. locator is free-text prose pointing into a paper ('Sec 3.3', 'eq. (1)', 'slide 11', 167 distinct of 180), and a pointer into a document does not own the item's type. `kind` belongs to the method/equation row itself, already determined by the real key (doc_id, seq).

subject: locator,seq
justification: Also witnessed by exactly one colliding group over 180 rows -- ('Section 3', seq=4, 2 rows). Worse than the previous candidate semantically: `seq` is a per-document ordinal, meaningless when crossed with a locator string from a different paper, so the pair names nothing in the modelled world. Free-text locator (167 distinct of 180) plus an ordinal is near-unique by construction.

subject: model
value: One method or equation extracted from one document, at a fixed position in that document's ordered list of extracted techniques.
justification: The DDL pairs a surrogate id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY with doc_id plus seq INTEGER NOT NULL, and the data shows seq restarting at 1 per document (ids 1-6 belong to doc 1, 7-12 to doc 2); v_methods orders by publication_year then seq. So (doc_id, seq) is the intended natural key of a per-document ordered list. Rejected uniqueness subjects: name — docs 2 and 3 are a paper and its own supplement, exactly the pair that would legitimately label the same technique twice; doc_id,locator and locator,seq — locator TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '' means blank locators collide by construction, and two methods routinely cite overlapping sections; description is free prose whose uniqueness over 22 rows is incidental. Atomicity: name is the label of a row that already carries exactly one kind, locator and description, so it names one thing however much mathematical punctuation it contains. Scope invariant — (doc_id, seq) identifying a method has no snapshot quality; only the parent document set is current-state. No mvd subjects were raised and observed_mvds is empty.

subject: links
justification: links is the free-text document-level summary of how a paper maps to our code ('conservative distance bounds for field/SDF evaluation (loose)') -- 33 distinct values over 43 rows. The only repeated value is the sentinel 'none' (11 rows), so the entire FD rests on those 11 rows all being tier 'off-theme'. The correlation is not even total: 12 rows are off-theme, and measured, exactly 1 off-theme row has real links prose rather than 'none'. It is also causally backwards -- the agent assigns score (1-10) and derives tier, then writes the prose summary; the prose does not own the tier. Near-unique free-text determinant over a small table.

subject: model
value: The single applicability ranking of one document under this catalog's ranking lens, with its score, tier band and written reason.
justification: The DDL declares doc_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES documents(id): exactly one ranking row per document. scope TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'applicability' is constant across all six rows and mirrors manifest.json's single ranking_lens, so (doc_id, scope) is a superkey rather than a second candidate key, and the discovered '[] -> scope' partial dependency is only that constant. The uniqueness subject links is rejected by its own DEFAULT '' — blank links collide by construction — and reason is free prose whose uniqueness over six rows is incidental; both are annotation payload, not identity. Worth recording though it does not touch the key: MANIFEST.md's legend ('render-relevant (>=6), conceptual-seed (3-5), off-theme (1-2)') makes score -> tier a genuine intended dependency, confirmed by every row (6,7,7 render-relevant; 3,5,5 conceptual-seed), so doc_id -> score -> tier is a real 3NF transitive dependency that a score-band lookup would remove. Scope invariant: one ranking per document with a banded tier holds in every legal state; only the parent document set is snapshot-dependent. No mvd subjects.

The uniqueness subject links is rejected by its own DEFAULT '' — blank links collide by construction — and reason is free prose whose uniqueness over six rows is incidental; both are annotation payload, not identity. Worth recording though it does not touch the key: MANIFEST.md's legend ('render-relevant (>=6), conceptual-seed (3-5), off-theme (1-2)') makes score -> tier a genuine intended dependency, confirmed by every row (6,7,7 render-relevant; 3,5,5 conceptual-seed), so doc_id -> score -> tier is a real 3NF transitive dependency that a score-band lookup would remove.
